title: Commerce Ministry Organises Series of Workshops on Opportunities Arising from Free Trade Agreements (FTAs)
subtitle:
India’s Preferential Market Access Expands to USD 70 Trillion, Expected to Reach USD 85 Trillion
Commerce Secretary Shri Rajesh Agarwal Highlights Global Market Opportunities for Rajasthan’s Gems, Jewellery, Textiles and Handicrafts
Rajasthan Targets ₹1.5 Lakh Crore in Exports by 2029, with Exports Reaching USD 11.18 Billion in 2025–26
FTA Workshop Held in Dehradun; Uttarakhand’s Exports Rise to ₹13,802 Crore
body_text: The Ministry of Commerce and Industry organised outreach initiatives in Jaipur and Dehradun on 27 November 2026 to familiarise exporters, entrepreneurs and Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) with opportunities arising from India’s Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and facilitate greater access to international markets. Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Minister, Shri Piyush Goyal, had earlier noted the expanding market access available to Indian businesses through recent Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and urged Indian businesses to utilize the opportunities opened by these agreements. He had said that India's preferential access to global markets, representing around USD 10 trillion in GDP until a few years ago, had expanded by an additional USD 60 trillion over the last four-and-a-half years, taking the total to approximately USD 70 trillion. With ongoing bilateral and multilateral trade engagements across eight to nine geographies, this was expected to expand to around USD 85 trillion, representing nearly 76 per cent of global GDP, over the next year to year-and-a-half. The Department of Commerce, Government of India, in collaboration with the Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO), the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) and the Government of Rajasthan organised an Exporters’ Outreach Session on Leveraging India’s Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) in Jaipur. Addressing exporters during the session, Commerce Secretary, Government of India, Shri Rajesh Agrawal spoke about the significant opportunities created by India’s FTAs and emphasised the need for Indian exporters, particularly MSMEs, to proactively leverage preferential market access. He encouraged exporters to identify sector-specific opportunities in FTA partner countries, participate in international exhibitions, develop overseas supply chains and explore emerging avenues such as cross-border e-commerce. Referring to Rajasthan’s strengths in sectors such as gems and jewellery, textiles, handicrafts, furniture and minerals, Shri Rajesh Agrawal urged businesses to translate these strengths into increased export opportunities. He also outlined the interventions under the Export Promotion Mission (EPM), including support for export credit, international exhibitions, testing and certification, overseas warehousing and logistics, aimed at enhancing the competitiveness of Indian exporters. Under the India-UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), customs duty on whole cumin seeds has been reduced from 5 per cent to zero, creating opportunities for Rajasthan’s farmers and farmer-producer organisations to expand their presence in the UAE market. For MSMEs and artisans engaged in textiles, handicrafts, jewellery and engineering, tariff preferences under the agreements improve price competitiveness in international markets. The 5 per cent duty on jewellery has also been removed under the UAE and Australia agreements, while the 2 to 4 per cent duty on jewellery has been removed under the United Kingdom agreement. The UK agreement also removes duties of up to 12 per cent on garments and 8 per cent on carpets. Under the EU agreement, duties of 12 per cent on cotton garments and bedlinen and 8 per cent on carpets will end upon its entry into force. India’s exports of goods and services reached USD 568.84 billion during April–October 2026, registering growth of 16.66 per cent. In October, exports of gems and jewellery grew by 40.06 per cent, handicrafts by 55.22 per cent, carpets by 20.64 per cent and readymade garments by 20.33 per cent. India has set an export target of USD 1 trillion for 2026–27. Rajasthan’s exports stood at USD 11.18 billion in 2025–26, led by engineering goods, gems and jewellery, and textiles and handicrafts. The State aims to achieve exports worth ₹1.5 lakh crore by 2029. The 100 per cent duty-free access provided under the New Zealand agreement opens new opportunities for MSMEs, artisans, farmers and women entrepreneurs. The agreement also provides Indian youth and professionals with 5,000 Temporary Employment Entry visas and 1,000 Working Holiday visas every year. The FTAs provide preferential access for labour-intensive products, supporting growth and employment in sectors such as textiles, apparel and leather goods. Under the UK agreement, workers are expected to gain new employment opportunities in labour-intensive sectors. Under the EFTA agreement, the EFTA States aim to raise their investment in India by USD 100 billion over 15 years and facilitate the generation of one million jobs within the same period. Joint Secretary, Department of Commerce, Government of India, Shri Mohit Yadav, spoke about Rajasthan’s distinctive role in leveraging India’s FTAs, given its inherent strengths across diverse export-oriented sectors. He noted that FTAs go beyond preferential market access and offer opportunities for technology transfer, joint ventures and investment partnerships, particularly in the context of the USD 100 billion investment commitment over 15 years under the India-EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA). Joint Director General of Foreign Trade, Jaipur, Shri Moin Afaque, outlined the utilisation of the trade agreements and the support available under the Export Promotion Mission, which has an outlay of ₹25,060 crore for 2025–26 to 2030–31. He also informed that the number of certificates eligible for reimbursement has increased to 600. MSME exporters from an additional 308 districts across 21 States and Union Territories are now eligible for reimbursement of transportation costs under EPM. Following the session, Shri Rajesh Agrawal interacted with exporters and industry representatives during an open-house discussion, addressing their concerns and issues relating to export opportunities and market access. He encouraged them to make greater use of the Trade Connect portal, engage with DGFT offices and Indian Missions abroad, and avail themselves of the various support mechanisms available under EPM to expand their presence in international markets. In another outreach initiative, a one-day State-Level Workshop on “Leveraging Free Trade Agreements” was organised in Dehradun by the Office of the Additional Director General of Foreign Trade (RA Delhi), Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India, in collaboration with the Industries Department, Government of Uttarakhand. The workshop aimed to connect the State’s micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), entrepreneurs and exporters with global markets by creating awareness about opportunities under India’s FTAs. The programme was attended by Minister for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), Government of Uttarakhand, Shri Bharat Singh Chaudhary, along with Joint Secretary, Department of Commerce, Government of India, Shri Amit Verma; Additional Director General of Foreign Trade, Government of India, Shri Nikhil Verma; and Director General and Commissioner of Industries, Government of Uttarakhand, Shri Saurabh Gaharwar. Representatives of leading trade and export promotion organisations, including PHDCCI, CII, EEPC, EPCH, APEDA and SEPC, along with entrepreneurs and exporters from across the State, participated in the workshop. Addressing the gathering, Shri Bharat Singh Chaudhary said that the workshop was an important initiative towards integrating Uttarakhand’s entrepreneurs, exporters, particularly MSME units into global supply chains. Referring to Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s vision of making India a developed nation by 2047, he noted that modern FTAs with countries such as Australia, the UAE and New Zealand are providing Indian products with zero-duty or preferential low-duty access to international markets. Speaking about the State’s industrial progress, Shri Chaudhary stated that Uttarakhand’s exports had increased from ₹10,836 crore in 2017–18 to ₹13,802 crore in 2025–26. Key contributors include pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, food processing, organic and herbal products, and handicrafts. He also informed that, through the ‘Invest Uttarakhand’ single-window portal, in-principle approvals had been granted to 6,932 projects involving capital investment of ₹70,397 crore over the past three years. Uttarakhand has also secured first rank in its category in NITI Aayog’s Export Preparedness Index (EPI) 2024 and the Investment Friendliness Index 2026. The Minister further informed that dedicated industrial parks are being established in Pauri, Chamoli and Almora to promote industrialisation in the hill districts. Following the establishment of the ₹194-crore Flatted Factory in Haridwar, similar plug-and-play facilities are proposed at Selaqui and Pantnagar. An Integrated Manufacturing Cluster (IMC) spread over 1,002 acres is also being developed at Khurpia, Kichha, at a cost of ₹1,100 crore. In addition, a Multi-Modal Logistics Park in Haridwar and a Land Customs Station at Banbasa are being developed to strengthen logistics and trade infrastructure. Initiatives such as ‘House of Himalayas’ and ‘Himadri’ are helping traditional handicrafts, Aipan art, millets and products of women’s self-help groups gain international recognition. Shri Saurabh Gaharwar, outlined Uttarakhand’s industrial ecosystem and roadmap for export promotion. Shri Amit Verma and Shri Nikhil Verma, provided detailed insights into India’s FTAs, tariff concessions, Rules of Origin (RoO), the Export Promotion Mission (EPM) and the ‘Districts as Export Hubs’ (DEH) initiative aimed at enhancing export competitiveness. The technical sessions featured experts from APEDA, SEPC, EPCH, EEPC, CII and PHDCCI, who discussed sector-specific export opportunities for Uttarakhand in agriculture, processed foods, handicrafts, services and engineering goods. Officials from the State Industries Department also briefed participants on financial incentives, quality certification support and logistics infrastructure available under the Uttarakhand Export Policy. The workshop concluded with an interactive question-and-answer session, during which exporters and industry representatives shared their queries and feedback directly with senior officials. The discussions provided a platform for stakeholders to understand the benefits of India’s FTAs and explore ways to expand Uttarakhand’s presence in international markets. The United Kingdom FTA, which came into force on 15 July 2026, provides zero-duty access on nearly 99 per cent of India’s exports. The agreement with Oman, effective from 1 June 2026, provides duty-free access for 99.38 per cent of India’s exports by value. India has also had FTAs with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Australia since 2022. Under the India-European Union (EU) agreement, duties will end upon its entry into force for 70.4 per cent of the EU’s tariff lines, covering 90.7 per cent of India’s export value, with a further 20.3 per cent of tariff lines being phased. The agreement is expected to come into effect in early 2027. With the United States, a framework for an interim agreement was announced on 7 February 2026, and negotiations are ongoing. The sixth round of negotiations with Canada was held from 11 to 20 November 2026, with the objective of securing an agreement that delivers tangible benefits to farmers, industries, businesses and Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs). Negotiations are also underway with Chile, Peru, Israel and the Eurasian Economic Union, as well as Mexico and other partners. The outreach initiatives reflect continued commitment to taking the benefits of India’s trade agreements to exporters across States, including MSMEs, women and young entrepreneurs. *** Abhishek Dayal/ Abhimanyu Panwar
